chief_complaint: excessive uncontrollable worry about everyday routines accompanied by muscle tension, restlessness, and insomnia
hpi_details: For 1 year, he has worried excessively about his health, finances, and family safety on most days and cannot reliably control the worry. He reports neck tension, restlessness, fatigue, and insomnia; GAD-7 score is 16. The symptoms impair concentration and work performance.
ideas: He wonders whether he has an anxiety disorder.
concerns: He worries that the symptoms will affect his job and relationships.
expectations: He wants an assessment, treatment options, and help sleeping.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Generalized Anxiety Disorder GAD Chronic Worry evaluation and management
core_concepts: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive anxiety and worry about multiple domains, occurring more days than not for at least 6 months, difficulty controlling it, associated symptoms, and clinically significant distress or impairment.
Assess depression, panic symptoms, trauma, obsessive symptoms, mania or hypomania, psychosis, substance and caffeine use, medical contributors, and medication effects.
Ask directly about suicidal ideation, self-harm, homicidal ideation, access to lethal means, and ability to care for self; arrange urgent emergency assessment when imminent risk is present.
First-line treatment includes CBT and an SSRI or SNRI chosen through shared decision-making; review adverse effects, activation, adherence, and response after initiation.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: excessive uncontrollable worry about everyday routines accompanied by muscle tension, restlessness, and insomnia
Key HPI features: one year of excessive, difficult-to-control worry about health, finances, and family safety with restlessness, neck tension, fatigue, insomnia, and work impairment; GAD-7 score 16.
Objective/Exam findings: assess vital signs, mental status, sleep, functional impairment, substance use, and focused physical findings for thyroid disease or other medical contributors.
common_misconceptions: A high GAD-7 score alone establishes the diagnosis.
All anxiety symptoms are psychiatric and require no review for substances, medicines, or medical causes.
Benzodiazepines are a routine long-term treatment without dependence or sedation risks.
Absence of volunteered suicidal thoughts means a safety assessment is unnecessary.
dangerous_errors: Missing suicidal intent, a plan, access to means, psychosis, inability to care for self, or risk to others; these require urgent safety assessment and escalation.
Missing alcohol, benzodiazepine, or other substance withdrawal, delirium, or mania presenting as anxiety.
Starting an antidepressant without counseling about early activation, sexual adverse effects, discontinuation symptoms, and follow-up monitoring.
Using sedating medication without considering driving, alcohol or opioid co-use, misuse risk, or the need for a time-limited plan.
management_principles: Confirm diagnostic criteria and impairment; use targeted testing only when history or examination suggests a medical cause, such as thyroid disease.
Offer CBT and discuss an SSRI or SNRI; start low and monitor clinical response, adverse effects, adherence, and suicide risk after medication changes.
Address sleep hygiene, exercise, caffeine reduction, alcohol and drug use, and practical supports.
Use urgent mental-health or emergency pathways for imminent self-harm or violence risk, inability to maintain safety, delirium, severe withdrawal, or suspected mania or psychosis.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Do not diagnose GAD if symptoms are better explained by a substance, medication, medical condition, another mental disorder, or a stressor-limited adjustment disorder.
Escalate if there is diagnostic uncertainty, significant comorbid depression or substance use, poor response to first-line treatment, or any safety concern.

reference_soap.subjective: 34-year-old man with one year of excessive, difficult-to-control worry about health, finances, and family safety on most days, with restlessness, neck tension, fatigue, insomnia, and work impairment. GAD-7 is 16. Assess mood, panic, trauma, mania, psychosis, substance use, and suicide, self-harm, and violence risk.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain vital signs, mental-status examination, functional assessment, substance-use history, and focused examination for medical contributors; order targeted tests only when indicated.
reference_soap.assessment: Probable generalized anxiety disorder; evaluate for depressive, panic, substance-induced, medical, trauma-related, obsessive-compulsive, and bipolar-spectrum conditions.
reference_soap.plan: If no urgent safety concern, offer CBT and shared decision-making about an SSRI or SNRI, with early follow-up for activation, adverse effects, adherence, and safety. Support sleep, exercise, and reduction of caffeine and substances. Urgently escalate for imminent risk, psychosis, mania, delirium, or withdrawal.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Generalized Anxiety Disorder GAD Chronic Worry
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for excessive uncontrollable worry about everyday routines accompanied by muscle tension, restlessness, and insomnia
Screen for safety risks, substance use, and medical or psychiatric conditions that can mimic anxiety
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.diagnosis: Generalized Anxiety Disorder GAD Chronic Worry
teaching.one_liner: Psychiatric evaluation for patient presenting with excessive uncontrollable worry about everyday routines accompanied by muscle tension, restlessness, and insomnia.

must_ask.say: Do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different things, more days than not?
Is it hard for you to control or stop the worrying once it starts?
Do you have muscle tension, feel restless, or get tired easily?
Has the worry made it hard for you to fall asleep or stay asleep?
Do you ever have sudden attacks of intense fear, or feel low in mood?
When anxiety feels overwhelming, have you had thoughts of harming yourself or someone else, or felt unable to keep yourself safe?
How much caffeine, alcohol, cannabis, or other substances do you use, and have you started or stopped any medicines recently?

history.answer: I've been feeling constantly on edge and overwhelmed by worry, and it has gotten to the point where I can't sleep or relax anymore.
I find myself worrying about almost everything—my health, paying bills, whether my family is safe, and minor everyday responsibilities.
This constant worrying has been going on for about a year now, happening almost every single day.
It is pretty much there all day in the background; once a worried thought enters my head, I cannot seem to turn it off or control it.
No, it is a constant, grinding worry throughout the day rather than sudden ten-minute waves of intense panic.
I don't get sudden episodes of a racing heart, choking sensations, dizziness, or a feeling that I'm about to die.
No, I don't avoid crowded places, buses, or stores out of fear of having an attack.
I feel a bit uneasy if I have to give a formal speech, but that's not what is bothering me; my anxiety happens even when I'm sitting alone at home.
history.topic: Anxiety in social or performance situations

history.answer: My neck and shoulders are always stiff and sore, I feel restless like I can't sit still, and I get exhausted very quickly.
My mind wanders constantly because of the worry, so it takes me twice as long to finish basic tasks at work.
It takes me hours to fall asleep because my mind keeps racing with worries, and I wake up feeling unrefreshed.
I get irritable with my wife and kid because of the exhaustion, and I worry I might make a big mistake at my job.
history.topic: Impact on relationships and daily life

history.answer: Nothing terrible happened, but regular pressures like household bills and quarterly deadlines at work feel completely unmanageable to me.
No, I've never experienced any terrifying trauma, and I don't have flashbacks, nightmares, or repetitive checking rituals.
I feel worn down and frustrated by this anxiety, but I don't feel hopeless, and I have never thought about ending my life or hurting myself.
No, my weight has been stable, and I haven't noticed heat intolerance, excessive sweating, or shaking hands.
No, I have never had chest tightness, shortness of breath, or fainting when I exercise.
I drink one small cup of brewed coffee in the morning to stay awake, and I don't drink energy drinks or take caffeine pills.
I have an occasional beer once or twice a month, but I never drink heavily and have never used sedatives, sleeping pills, or recreational drugs.
I've tried going for evening walks and listening to breathing exercises, but they only help for a few minutes before the racing thoughts return.
I wonder if this constant tension means I have an actual anxiety disorder rather than just everyday stress.
I'm really worried that this will spiral and ruin my job performance or damage my marriage.
I'm hoping you can tell me what's causing this, discuss treatment options, and help me finally get some sleep.
I have high blood pressure and mildly elevated cholesterol, but no other medical problems.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day in the morning for my blood pressure; I don't take any supplements or over-the-counter pills.
I don't have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I work as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my wife and our six-year-old child.
My mother always had what she called nervous stomach and worried a lot, but no one in my family was formally diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder.
